title: Pioneering Speaker Jones to retire, Schaufele moves on, and a zebra debate, in political notes
summary: Former House Speaker Adrienne Jones (D-Baltimore County), a pioneer, will not seek reelection this fall, self-described government nerd Andrew Schaufele leaves the comptroller's office after 20 years, and the House debates zebras, in political notes.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears and Christine Condon, Maryland Matters February 25, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears and Christine Condon, Maryland Matters February 25, 2026

The historic legislative career of Del. Adrienne Jones (D-Baltimore County) is coming to a close.

Jones, the first woman and first Black lawmaker to serve as House speaker, has filed to withdraw as a candidate in the 2026 election, according to state election officials.

Jones was first appointed to the House in 1997. She went on to win the next seven elections, and was speaker for the last six years, before she abruptly stepped down in December, while keeping her seat in the House.

Jones had intended to run this year to retain her seat in the district that covers a portion of western Baltimore County, and filed for reelection in June. But an undisclosed health issue derailed those plans. She has missed all but three days of the current session. A spokesperson for House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk said Jones is under a doctor’s care and her absence is excused.

Jones was one of three delegates to represent District 10, along with Dels. Jennifer White Holland and N. Scott Phillips, both Democrats, who have filed for reelection.

Among the four others who have also filed to run in the district is Jay Jalisi, a former two term state delegate. The General Assembly voted unanimously to reprimand Jalisi in 2019 for chronic abuse of staff and creating a toxic work environment. The allegations sustained in a Joint Committee on Legislative Ethics report stretched over a five-year period dating back to almost the start of his time in the House.

Jalisi ran for the Maryland Senate in 2022, but lost in the Democratic primary to current Sen. Ben Brooks.

Maryland’s chief deputy comptroller will leave the state’s tax collection agency this summer.

Andrew Schaufele, a nearly 20-year veteran of the office, is stepping down effective June 1.

“This is the hardest decision I’ve ever made — and I’ve made many tough ones in service to the State. I love this Agency,” Schaufele wrote in an email to colleagues.

Schaufele did not elaborate on his plans, but said he “accepted an opportunity that aligns with my professional goals, supports my continued growth, and — most importantly — serves my family’s needs.”

One of Schaufele’s early posts within the agency was as head of the Board of Revenue Estimates. It was there that he developed a reputation for a deep understanding of national economic trends and their effects on the state’s fiscal picture.

A self-proclaimed government nerd, Schaufele had a keen eye for the minutiae of revenue and economic forecasts and the ability to break those concepts down for the fiscally challenged, reporters included. Veterans of the press corps can remember Schaufele’s patient and detailed breakdown of how state finances could be affected by changes in the 2017 Tax Cuts for Jobs Act.

“My relationship with Andy predates my time as Comptroller,” Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D) said in a statement. “When I was serving as a Delegate, I had the privilege of working alongside Andy — then Director of the Bureau of Revenue Estimates — on legislation that we ultimately saw through to passage together. That experience gave me a clear picture of who he was: someone deeply committed to this work, collaborative to his core, and someone who made the people around him better. So when I arrived at this agency with a vision and a lot of ideas, I already knew I could trust him.”

Schaufele left the agency briefly in 2020 to work for a Washington, D.C., analytics company that helps governments develop tax fraud detection systems. He returned to the agency and the Board of Revenue Estimates after less than a year, and later served as a deputy to then-Comptroller Peter Franchot (D).

It’s a “black-and-white issue,” according to Del. Kevin Hornberger (R- Cecil).

The farmer in his county who owns zebras, and uses them to graze the fields and control weeds, should be allowed to get more zebras in the future — even though the Maryland General Assembly wants to ban them, along with kangaroos, and wallaroos and wallabies. (The bill, House Bill 53, includes exceptions for zoos, circuses and research facilities.)

Hornberger proposed an amendment to the bill that would allow the animals for agricultural uses, kicking off a nearly 15-minute zebra discussion in the House of Delegates on Wednesday morning.

Del. N. Scott Phillips (D- Baltimore County) urged the delegates to vote against the amendment, earning a disappointed groan from the crowd, who had waited eagerly for an uncooperative machine to scan the amendment.

Phillips pointed out that in 2021 a group of five zebras escaped from an Upper Marlboro farm and roamed the county “wreaking havoc” for months before they were captured. He indicated that there might be room for amending the bill, but that Hornberger’s exemption was too wide-ranging.

“Not only is it — we believe — inappropriate to have zebras, because there are all types of options in terms of animals that can graze and clear, but the other piece is that the amendment in and of itself is overly broad,” Phillips said.

In the end, Hornberger agreed to withdraw his amendment, with the promise from Democrats that they would work with him to amend the bill once it heads to the Senate. And with that, the bill passed on second reader.

But when the morning’s session concluded, House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D- Prince George’s & Anne Arundel) had some words of advice for the Cecil County Republican.

“I got up on this floor many years ago to defend baby bears, cubs, from traps. And let me tell you, I heard about that for years to come. Good luck to you,” she said.
